“They know how clever he is. He'll get life. Nothing less than life for the Artful.”

“What do you mean by ‘lagging’ and ‘a lifer’?” Mr. Bolter demanded. “What's the point of talking to me like that? Why can't you use words I understand?”

Fagin was about to explain these mysterious terms in ordinary language. Mr. Bolter would then have learned that they meant being sent to a penal colony for life. But the conversation stopped when Master Bates entered, his hands in his trouser pockets and his face twisted into an expression of grief that was almost funny.

“It's all over, Fagin,” Charley said, after he and the newcomer had been introduced.

“What do you mean?”

“They've found the gentleman who owns the box. Two or three more people are coming to identify the Artful, and he's booked for a voyage abroad,” Master Bates replied. “I'll need a full suit of mourning, Fagin, and a black hatband, to visit him before he starts his travels. To think of Jack Dawkins—clever old Jack—the Dodger—the Artful Dodger—being sent overseas for an ordinary little snuffbox worth next to nothing! I always thought he'd manage at least a gold watch, chain and seals. Oh, why couldn't he have stripped some rich old gentleman of all his valuables and gone off like a gentleman, instead of a common thief with no honour or glory?”

Having expressed these feelings for his unfortunate friend, Master Bates dropped into the nearest chair, looking bitterly disappointed and miserable.

“What do you mean, saying he has no honour or glory?” Fagin cried, shooting an angry glance at his pupil. “Wasn't he always the finest among you? Could any of you match him, or even come close, on any job? Well?”

“Not one,” Master Bates answered, his voice rough with sorrow. “Not one.”

“Then what are you talking about?” Fagin snapped. “What are you crying for?”

“Because none of that's on the record, is it?” said Charley. His regret had made him angry enough to defy his elderly friend completely. “Because it can't be included in the charges. Because nobody will ever know half of what he was. What will they say about him in the Newgate Calendar? Perhaps he won't even get into that book of criminals. Oh, what a blow! What a terrible blow!”

“Ha, ha!” Fagin cried. He held out his right hand and turned to Mr. Bolter, chuckling so hard that he shook as though afflicted with tremors. “See how proud they are of their profession, my dear.”

Almost a year had passed since my father's return, and the seasons had nearly completed their cycle. It was late May now; the woods wore their freshest green, and the fields smelled sweetly of newly cut grass. I hoped that the mild air and nature's lovely face might help me awaken gentler emotions in him, bringing him feelings of peace and love before I sought the confidence I was determined to gain.

So I chose one of these evenings to make my attempt. I asked him to walk with me and guided him into a nearby beech wood, where the light shade protected us from the dazzling, slanting rays of the setting sun. After we had walked silently for a while, I sat with him on a mossy mound. Strange as it seems, I can still see the place: many of the slender, smooth trunks were entwined with ivy, its glossy, dark green leaves contrasting with the white bark and pale foliage of the young beech shoots growing from the parent trees. Moss mingled with the short grass, which was partly covered by last autumn's dead leaves, blown into little heaps here and there. A few moss-covered stumps stood nearby. The breeze gently moved the leaves, and through their green canopy the sky shone blue. As evening deepened, the sun reddened the distant trunks, the wind died away completely, and a few birds flew past towards their nightly resting places.

This was where we sat together. When you hear everything that happened—all the terrible things that tore at our souls even in that peaceful setting, which might have been a paradise to us but for strange passions—you will understand why I remember it. I studied it in the hope that its calm would steady me, giving me persuasive words as well as courage. I saw all these details and noted them almost absently while trying to arrange my thoughts into a suitable order for what I intended. My heart raced as I worked myself up to address him. I had resolved that I would not be turned away, yet I trembled to think of the effect my words might have on him. At last, with considerable hesitation, I began:

“Your kindness towards me, my dearest father, and the affection—the overwhelming affection—you showed me when you first returned will, I hope, excuse my daring to speak to you with the tender love of a daughter, but also with the freedom of a friend and an equal.”

“He was handed over to you. You see, I know the circumstances?”

“That is certainly true,” Defarge said. While his wife knitted and softly sang, a seemingly accidental touch of her elbow had told him that he should answer, but keep his replies short.

“His daughter came to you,” the spy continued, “and took him from your care to England, accompanied by a tidy gentleman in brown. What was his name? He wore a small wig. Lorry, from Tellson and Company's bank.”

“That is true,” Defarge repeated.

“What interesting memories!” said the spy. “I have met Doctor Manette and his daughter in England.”

“Have you?” Defarge said.

“You don't hear much of them these days?” asked the spy.

“No,” said Defarge.

“In fact,” madame interrupted, looking up from her knitting and her little song, “we hear nothing of them. We were told they had arrived safely, and perhaps received another letter, or perhaps two. But since then they have gradually gone their way through life, and we have gone ours. We haven't kept in touch.”

“Of course, madame,” the spy replied. “She is going to marry.”

“Going to?” madame repeated. “She was pretty enough to have married years ago. You English seem cold to me.”

“Oh! You know I'm English.”

“I can hear that your tongue is English,” madame answered, “and I suppose the man belongs to the same country as his tongue.”

He did not consider this recognition a compliment, but made the best of it and laughed it off. After finishing his cognac, he continued:

“Yes, Miss Manette is getting married. Her husband won't be English, though. Like her, he was born in France. And speaking of Gaspard—ah, poor Gaspard! It was cruel, so cruel!—it is curious that she is marrying the nephew of the Marquis whose death sent Gaspard so many feet up into the air on the gallows. In other words, she is marrying the present Marquis. But he lives quietly in England, where nobody knows his rank. There he is simply Mr. Charles Darnay. His mother's family name is D'Aulnais.”

Madame Defarge kept knitting steadily, but the news clearly affected her husband. Behind the little counter he tried to occupy himself by striking a light and lighting his pipe, yet his distress showed, and his hand shook. The spy would hardly have deserved his calling if he had failed to notice and remember this.

Having at least gained this one advantage, whatever it might be worth, and with no customers arriving to offer another opportunity, Mr. Barsad paid for his drink and left. Before going, he took care to say politely that he looked forward to the pleasure of seeing Monsieur and Madame Defarge again.
